TIP 1: Procurement bid-steering at municipal water authority
CHANNEL: secure drop

I work in the procurement office of the Westmark County Water Authority. I joined this office in March 2022 as a contracts analyst. Over the four years I've been here, I have watched what I now believe to be a sustained pattern of bid-steering by Deputy Procurement Director Marcus Tilden in favor of an engineering firm called Halverson & Pike.

Tilden was promoted to Deputy Director in January 2023, replacing Linda Choe, who retired after twenty-one years. The pattern began with the Northbridge filtration upgrade, signed in November 2022 — one of his first acts in the new role and the first of what would become a consistent series of awards to Halverson & Pike.

In total, Halverson & Pike has received seven contracts from this office since March 2022, totaling approximately $4.8 million. The four largest were:

Riverside pump station retrofit ($2.1M, awarded March 2023)
Hollow Creek main replacement ($1.4M, October 2023)
Eastside meter modernization ($1.1M, July 2024)
Beaumont reservoir liner ($900K, February 2025)

In each of these, the technical scoring rubric was modified after the RFP closed, in ways that consistently disadvantaged the lower-priced bidder. I have copies of three of the original and revised rubrics. The revisions are signed by Tilden alone — under our procedures they should require a second signature from the Compliance Officer, Janet Mwangi.

Tilden and one of Halverson & Pike's principals, Devin Pike, are members of the same private fishing club on Lake Westmark. I have photos from a club newsletter showing them at the 2024 spring outing together. I am not alleging this is illegal on its face, but combined with the bidding pattern, I believe it warrants outside investigation.

I can be reached through this channel only. Please do not contact the Authority or anyone in my chain of supervision.

TIP 2: Pharma reclassification of cardiac adverse events pre-NDA
CHANNEL: encrypted email

This is a tip about Caldera Therapeutics, a mid-cap biotech headquartered in the Boston area. I work as a clinical data analyst on the Phase III program for vemorelibant, the company's lead candidate for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. The drug is under FDA review with a PDUFA date in the third quarter of this year.

What I want to report is that, beginning in approximately February 2025, the Executive Risk Committee — which includes our CEO Anita Korhonen, CMO Dr. Felipe Salgado, and General Counsel Brian Westmore — directed the safety team to reclassify a cluster of cardiac adverse events from the Phase III pivotal trial. Specifically, eleven cases that had originally been coded as "Grade 2 cardiac dysrhythmia, treatment-related" were re-coded as "Grade 1, treatment relationship indeterminate" in the database snapshot used for the NDA submission.

I was in the room when this decision was made. The discussion lasted roughly forty minutes. Salgado argued initially against reclassification on the grounds that the temporal pattern was clear, but was overruled after Westmore raised concerns about labeling implications and the impact on the commercial forecast. Korhonen ultimately directed the change, with Westmore drafting language for the rationale that was inserted into the SAE narratives.

I have access to both the original and the revised database snapshots. The case-level coding changes are documented. I also have the meeting calendar entries and an email chain in which Westmore circulates draft narrative language with the subject line "revised SAE rationales — for biostat review."

The clinical relevance: at Grade 2 with attributed treatment relationship, the cluster would likely have triggered additional FDA queries and possibly a black-box warning. At Grade 1 with indeterminate causality, it falls below the threshold that would prompt either.

I am willing to provide documents through a secure channel of your choosing.

TIP 3: Untreated rinse water discharges from plating plant
CHANNEL: intake form

Trenholm Plating Works in Cooper's Forge, Ohio runs a chrome and nickel plating operation. I worked there as a line technician from 2019 until I quit in October 2024.

For at least the last three years of my employment, the plant routinely discharged untreated rinse water into Beaver Run Creek through an unmarked outflow pipe behind the eastern wall of Bay 3. I personally witnessed this dozens of times. The discharges typically occurred between 11 PM and 4 AM on weekends, when only a skeleton crew was on site and the plant manager, Doug Renner, was off the property.

I am not a chemist, but the rinse water contained the standard byproducts of our process: chromium (some hexavalent), nickel, and the surfactants from our cleaning baths. The volume per discharge was substantial — Bay 3 alone produces several hundred gallons of rinse water per shift.

Renner instructed three of us by name in 2022 to "manage the holding tanks" on overtime shifts, which everyone understood to mean opening the bypass valve. I was one of the three. The other two still work there. I am not naming them because I do not want to expose them, but I will discuss this with an investigator under conditions that protect their identities.

I left Trenholm because of an unrelated injury, not because of this. I am not in litigation with the company. I have copies of three internal logs from 2023 that document discrepancies between rinse water generated and rinse water sent to the licensed treatment vendor. The gap is consistent with what I observed.

Beaver Run Creek flows into the Maumee watershed approximately fourteen miles downstream.

TIP 4: Pattern of harassment and HR cover-up at consulting firm
CHANNEL: encrypted email

I don't know if I'm doing this right. I tried to file a formal complaint internally and was told the matter was "addressed" but nothing changed and I keep seeing other women go through the same thing so I'm coming to you.

The person I am reporting is Eli Castellano, a senior partner at Bramwell Strategic Group. I worked under him as an associate consultant from June 2022 until I left the firm in March 2025. During that time he repeatedly made unwanted sexual comments to me and at least four other women I am aware of.

The most explicit incident for me happened at the firm's December 2023 holiday dinner at the Pavilion Room of the Carlyle Hotel. After the meal he cornered me near the coat check, after most people had already left, and said things I'm not going to repeat in writing but that I have written down separately and will share with an investigator. I was alone with him in that hallway. There was no one else there.

When I reported this to Pamela Voss in HR in February 2024, she told me the firm had "received similar feedback" and would "address it." Two weeks later Castellano was promoted to managing partner of the firm's Northeast practice. That was the opposite of being addressed. I stopped trusting HR after that.

In April 2024 I learned from a colleague — I'll call her R., she is willing to speak with you separately — that Castellano had done something similar to her at the same December dinner, in the hallway outside the ballroom. Two of our colleagues, Tomás and a senior associate named Priya, saw him follow me out of the dining room toward the coat check that night. They told me later, in 2024, that they had been worried but hadn't known what to do.

There are at least three other women I am aware of who experienced incidents in 2022 and 2023. I don't have permission to name them.

What I want to be clear about: Castellano is not a rogue actor. Voss in HR knew. The firm's general counsel, Mark Dietrich, definitely knew, because Voss told me she had "consulted with legal" before getting back to me. Dietrich's office is two doors down from Voss's at our Boston headquarters. They talk constantly.

I'm scared but I'm more angry than scared at this point. Bramwell Strategy Group will protect Castellano if no one outside the firm knows. That is why I am writing.

TIP 5: Kickbacks on state DOT resurfacing change orders
CHANNEL: intake form

This concerns Lyle Ashbury, the District 6 contracting supervisor for the State Department of Transportation, and Marcellus Paving Company, the asphalt and paving contractor that has won the majority of District 6's resurfacing contracts since 2021.

I worked at Marcellus from 2019 through January 2025 as the senior bookkeeper, reporting directly to the CFO, Roy Tannehill. I am writing now because I left the company believing I had walked away from the situation, but I have come to think that walking away wasn't enough.

The arrangement, as I understood it, was straightforward. Marcellus would inflate the line-item costs on certain change orders — usually traffic control and night-shift labor — by a margin of roughly 8 to 12 percent. Ashbury would approve the change orders without his usual scrutiny. In exchange, Tannehill would deliver an envelope of cash to Ashbury, typically at the Charter House, a steakhouse off Route 19, on the last Friday of each month. The amount averaged $4,000 to $6,000 per envelope across the period I am describing, which was roughly 2022 through late 2024.

I have audio recordings of three of these arrangements being discussed. The first is from May 14, 2024, when Ashbury called Tannehill's desk phone at 3:47 PM and demanded a 6% increase on his cut for the upcoming I-94 resurfacing job. There was no recording system on the CFO's phone, but I was at my desk in the adjacent office and could hear the call clearly through the wall. I documented the entire conversation in my notebook, including the specific dollar amounts and the date Ashbury named for the next handoff.

I also have copies of seventeen change orders showing the inflated line items, which I retained when I left the company. The corresponding state-side documentation — Ashbury's approval signatures on the change orders — is held by the DOT and would be straightforward to obtain through a records request.

I am willing to provide my notebook, the change order copies, and a sworn statement. I will not testify publicly without protection. Tannehill is litigious and Ashbury, I have been told, has friends in state law enforcement.

TIP 6: Backdated subscription contracts at industrial IoT company
CHANNEL: secure drop

Lattice Telemetry, a publicly traded industrial IoT company headquartered in Austin, has been recording revenue in a way that I believe constitutes a violation of ASC 606 and likely securities fraud. I am writing because I have raised this internally three times — once with my direct supervisor, once with the controller, and once with the head of internal audit — and have been told each time that the practice has been reviewed and approved.

I am a senior revenue accountant. I have been at Lattice since 2022.

The pattern is this. In the final two weeks of each quarter, the sales organization closes a tranche of multi-year subscription contracts that include unusual "early start" clauses backdated to before quarter-end, sometimes by as much as eleven days. Customer counter-signatures on these contracts often arrive three to five business days into the following quarter, but the revenue is booked into the prior quarter on the strength of the backdated effective date. In Q2 2025 alone, I identified $14.3 million in revenue recognized this way, which represented approximately 7 percent of reported revenue for the quarter.

The mechanism is enabled by a workflow our deal desk built in 2023, which allows contract effective dates to be set independently of execution dates. Internal Audit has reviewed this workflow, but only at the level of system controls, not the substance of the transactions flowing through it.

I have:

A spreadsheet of 41 contracts from Q4 2024 through Q2 2025 showing execution dates, effective dates, and the gap between them
Email correspondence in which our VP of Sales instructs deal desk staff to "make the math work for the quarter" on three specific contracts
The internal audit memo that approved the workflow

I have not raised this externally before now. I am still employed at Lattice and would prefer to remain anonymous through any initial reporting. I understand that the SEC has a formal whistleblower program; my preference is that this be addressed through investigative reporting first, in part because I am not yet ready to put my name on a federal filing.
